claims.text: The starting alloy is a single-phase solid solution containing at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
Rapid cooling of the as-cast alloy produces a relatively random atomic distribution with minimal local chemical order.
Changing annealing conditions can systematically vary local chemical order without changing the alloy's overall composition.
Different annealing treatments induce measurable variations in local chemical ordering.
The degree of local chemical ordering governs superconducting behavior in the proposed alloy.
Local chemical ordering modulates the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Local chemical ordering modulates the electron-scattering rate.
Changes in the Fermi-level density of states and electron-scattering rate affect electron–phonon coupling strength.
Enhanced local ordering increases the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Enhanced local ordering improves electron–phonon coupling and thereby promotes Cooper-pair formation.
Excessive chemical disorder increases electron scattering, which can suppress superconductivity.
An optimal intermediate degree of local order exists at which beneficial electronic effects outweigh scattering-related detriments.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, controlled slow annealing that enhances local order will increase the superconducting transition temperature.
Controlled slow annealing that enhances local order will improve superconducting properties relative to the as-cast baseline.
If local order becomes too pronounced, further transition-temperature enhancement may cease or the transition temperature may be suppressed because of increased scattering.
The hypothesis is limited to alloys that remain single-phase solid solutions without segregation, precipitation, or secondary-phase formation while local order is varied.
X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy can quantify the annealing-induced changes in local order relevant to the experiment.
Residual resistivity ratio can serve as a proxy for electron scattering in the tested samples.
A lack of systematic correlation between independently measured local order and transition temperature or resistivity would falsify the proposed ordering-mediated mechanism.
An invariant transition temperature despite significant changes in local order would falsify the proposed hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The mechanism attributes increased scattering to excessive chemical disorder and portrays ordering as improving electron–phonon coupling, whereas the predicted outcome says excessively pronounced local order may suppress T_c because of increased scattering. No explanation is provided for why greater ordering would increase scattering.
